captures.text: Figure 1: A map for following how a choice takes shape. The steps can overlap or repeat; green arrows show how learning can influence later decisions.

Table 8.1: System 1 and System 2 compared on the same dimensions Feature System 1 System 2 Cognitive demands Relatively autonomous; little demand on working memory Depends on working memory and cognitive control Typical speed and effort Often fast and effortless, especially with practice Often slower and more effortful Common contributions Supplies impressions, habitual responses, and skilled recognition Maintains goals, compares alternatives, simulates, and checks responses Sources of error Misleading cues or poorly learned associations can supply a convincing answer Limited capacity or selective reasoning can leave an error intact or defend it

Figure 8.2: System 1 and System 2 name clusters of processing features. Automatic processes often supply candidate answers; working-memory-dependent processes can sometimes inspect, inhibit, redirect, or train them.

Table 9.1: When affect, availability, and representativeness help or mislead Shortcut Useful when Misleads when Corrective Affect Feeling summarizes relevant, repeated experience. Mood or identity spills into an unrelated forecast. Name the feeling, then estimate probability separately. Availability Memory samples the environment fairly. News, vividness, recency, or repetition make selected cases easier to recall. Compare the memorable case with the full record of relevant opportunities. Representativeness The prototype contains features validated for the target prediction. Surface fit substitutes for prevalence or diagnosticity. Add the base rate and ask what alternatives produce the same features.
Figure 9.3: A category resemblance can suggest a hypothesis; updating its probability requires the prior and evidence that distinguishes competing explanations.

Table 15.1: Three forms of overconfidence require different comparisons Form of overconfidence Comparison required Useful feedback Overestimation Predicted versus measured performance Record estimates and outcomes on the same scale across comparable tasks. Overplacement Predicted versus measured relative standing Specify the comparison group and criterion, then check the predicted rank. Overprecision Stated certainty versus accuracy across comparable judgments Compare prediction-interval coverage with its stated level, or probability judgments with observed event frequencies.

Table 39.2: Components within COM-B and B=MAP; the frameworks overlap but organize the diagnosis differently Framework Component Diagnostic question COM-B Capability Does the person have the psychological and physical capacity, including the necessary knowledge and skills? COM-B Opportunity Do external conditions provide the time, access, tools, permission, and social support needed? COM-B Motivation Do reflective intentions and automatic processes support the action? B=MAP Motivation Is the person sufficiently willing to act at this moment, given how easy or difficult it is? B=MAP Ability Is the action easy enough now, given its demands on time, effort, money, and the existing routine? B=MAP Prompt What calls for the action at the moment it is feasible?

Table 39.3: Four features of a digital engagement loop and their safeguards Loop feature Helpful use Capture risk Agency safeguard Prompt Timely medication or coordination prompt Continuous interruption and anxiety cue User-controlled timing and batching Easy action Removes needless access friction One-tap entry into an endless loop Visible stopping point and deliberate continuation Variable feedback Makes practice interesting Repeated checking for uncertain social reward Bounded sessions and honest expectations Investment Saves progress or supports relationships Sunk data and streaks make exit painful Portability, pause, easy cancellation

Table 39.4: Behavior-change tools and their best uses Tool Best used when… Example Implementation intention The goal is clear but follow-through fails at the critical moment. If I feel the urge to explain during feedback, then I ask one clarifying question first. WOOP Positive intention needs an honest obstacle and a concrete plan. Wish: prepare earlier. Outcome: calm negotiation. Obstacle: vague starting point. Plan: if unclear, then write three interests. Friction design The behavior is sensitive to small barriers or ease. Phone outside bedroom; saved card removed; document opened before leaving work. Temptation bundling The desired behavior has delayed benefits and needs immediate reward. Only listen to a favorite audiobook while walking. Precommitment Future states predictably defeat current intentions. Restricted-access savings; an app block that cannot be immediately disabled; a prepaid class with a cancellation penalty. Context change Old cues keep recruiting the old behavior. Use a new study location, new commute, new meeting script, or new semester routine. BRAIN observation prompts A mild everyday impulse is present and a pause may help choice. Use Chapter 21’s classroom mnemonic to notice the impulse and pause before acting. Relapse plan A missed repetition could become identity proof. If I miss once, then I restart at the next cue with the smallest version.
